blocks.html: The point of a simulator is not to look like a network. It is to explain what a network did.
The Concept First

NetSim runs entirely in the browser. It has no backend, no containers and no real kernels. It is a discrete-event simulator: devices, links and packets are objects in TypeScript, and every packet is an event on a clock.

That design gives three things a real network cannot:

  • Determinism: the same topology and the same actions produce the same result.
  • Inspectability: every packet can be paused, stepped and explained.
  • Portability: it runs on a locked-down laptop or a Chromebook with no install.

The trade-off is scope. NetSim simulates a curated subset of IPv4 networking: L2 switching, ARP, static and RIP routing, ICMP, TCP handshakes, UDP, DHCP, DNS, HTTP, stateful firewalls and NAT. It does not simulate IPv6, OSPF/BGP, TLS, real payloads or performance.

It is a teaching and design tool. It is not a packet-accurate emulator.
Understanding Through a Flight Simulator

A flight simulator does not reproduce every bolt in the aircraft. It reproduces the instruments and the decisions that matter for a flight lesson.

NetSim reproduces the decisions that matter for a networking lesson: addressing, routing, switching, firewalls and services.
Discovering the Tool with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Separate the Model from the World

Ask the AI to list what the simulator can and cannot prove.

NetSim simulates ARP, IPv4 routing, ICMP, TCP, UDP, DHCP, DNS, HTTP,
stateful firewalls and NAT.
It does not simulate IPv6, OSPF/BGP, TLS, real payloads or performance.

For each capability, write one question the simulator can answer and one
it cannot. Do not claim the simulator proves more than its model.

A good answer keeps the model boundary visible.

Exploration 2: Find the Explainability

Ask why a deterministic simulator can explain a drop.

A real kernel drops a packet silently. A deterministic simulator can name
the rule, the interface and the exact event. Explain why that matters for
teaching and for firewall design.

The explanation is the pedagogical advantage.

Exploration 3: Choose the Use

Ask which tasks fit.

List five networking tasks. For each, say whether NetSim is a good fit,
a partial fit or the wrong tool. Include production performance testing,
firewall rule design, protocol learning and incident response.

The answer is a scope decision, not a sales pitch.
From Concept to Practice

A tool-fit record:

Task Fit Why
Learn ARP Strong Visible packets and tables
Design a firewall Strong Rule model and verdict log
Test throughput Poor No performance modelling
Learn OSPF Poor Not simulated
Teach subnetting Strong Immediate feedback
Build Task
Open the demo topology. Pause the clock, step through one ping, and name every device the packet touched.
Classroom Connection
The simulator is a glass box. Students can see the packet, the table and the rule. That visibility is the lesson.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 1.1 (Level 1). List three things NetSim can explain that a real network cannot. Exercise 1.2 (Level 2). Name three things NetSim does not simulate. Exercise 1.3 (Level 3). Classify five tasks as good, partial or wrong fit. Exercise 1.4 (Level 4). Explain the trade-off between determinism and realism. Exercise 1.5 (Level 5). Write a one-paragraph scope statement for using NetSim in a course.
Chapter Summary

• NetSim is a browser-based discrete-event simulator.
  • It is deterministic, inspectable and portable.
  • It simulates a curated IPv4 subset, not everything.
  • The explanation of a drop is the pedagogical advantage.
  • Choose the tool for the question.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Named the model boundary
  • [ ] Stepped through one packet
  • [ ] Classified one task
  • [ ] Explained the trade-off
  • [ ] Wrote a scope statement
Your Learning Journal

1. What did the animation make visible?
  2. What is outside the model?
  3. Where would you still use a real lab?
Next Steps
The tool is scoped. The next chapter builds a topology.
A topology is a set of devices, links and addresses that can be reasoned about.
The Concept First

NetSim's device palette has six types:

  • Host: one interface.
  • Server: one interface, with service editors.
  • Switch: eight ports, L2 forwarding and VLANs.
  • Router: four interfaces, IPv4 forwarding.
  • Firewall: four interfaces and nftables base chains.
  • Wi-Fi AP: a bridge with wireless client links.

Drag a device onto the canvas, or click to drop one. Cable two devices by dragging from a dot on one to a dot on the other.

Addressing can be done in two places: the Inspector fields or a terminal. Both use the same engine, so the result is identical.

The starting topology is a claim about the network. Leave unconfigured what the student must configure. Configure what the scenario provides.
Understanding Through a Model Railway

A model railway is not a real railway. It is a track plan, a set of trains and a power supply that lets you test a timetable.

The topology is the track plan. The addresses and routes are the timetable.
Discovering Topology with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Choose the Devices

Ask the AI to translate a scenario into devices.

Scenario: two subnets, each with two hosts, joined by a router, with a
firewall between the subnets and an internet host.

List the devices, interfaces and links. Mark which device needs a route
and which needs a firewall rule.

A good answer separates the topology from the configuration.

Exploration 2: Plan the Addressing

Ask for an address plan.

Plan IPv4 addressing for two LANs, a transit link and an internet host.
Use private ranges. For each device and interface, give the address,
prefix and default gateway.

The plan is the contract before the commands.

Exploration 3: Find the Minimum Topology

Ask what can be removed.

Here is a topology: [paste it]
Remove devices and links that do not change the question being tested.
Explain what each removal changes.

A smaller topology is easier to debug and grade.
From Concept to Practice

A topology record:

Device Type Interfaces Addresses Role
pc1 Host eth0 192.168.1.10/24 LAN client
sw1 Switch 8 ports none L2 segment
r1 Router eth0, eth1 .1 on each LAN Gateway
fw1 Firewall 4 ports outside/inside Policy
web Server eth0 203.0.113.10/24 Public service
Build Task
Build a two-host, one-switch network. Address both hosts, cable them and ping. Then add a router and a second subnet.
Classroom Connection
A topology that fits on one screen is easier to discuss. Start small; add one device only when the question needs it.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 2.1 (Level 1). Name the six device types. Exercise 2.2 (Level 2). Build a two-host network. Exercise 2.3 (Level 3). Plan addressing for two LANs. Exercise 2.4 (Level 4). Add a router and default routes. Exercise 2.5 (Level 5). Reduce a topology to the minimum that tests the question.
Chapter Summary

• A topology is devices, links and addresses.
  • The palette covers hosts, servers, switches, routers, firewalls and APs.
  • Address in the Inspector or the terminal; the engine is the same.
  • Leave the learning to the student.
  • Start small.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Built a two-host network
  • [ ] Cabled the devices
  • [ ] Addressed the interfaces
  • [ ] Added a router
  • [ ] Drew the topology record
Your Learning Journal

1. Which device was easiest to miswire?
  2. Where did the addressing plan help?
  3. What would you remove next time?
Next Steps
The topology is built. The next chapter configures it with real syntax.
NetSim accepts a curated subset of real Linux syntax and errors loudly on everything else.
The Concept First

The terminal supports a subset of iproute2, nft, iptables, DHCP, DNS, HTTP and socket commands.

Common commands:

ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0
ip link set eth0 up
ip route add default via 192.168.1.1
ip neigh
ping 192.168.1.20
traceroute 203.0.113.10
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

A firewall is a router with nftables base chains declared. Rules can be written in nft or iptables; both compile to one internal model and list in both dialects.

The important design choice: unsupported syntax produces an explicit netsim: "..." is not supported error. The tool never silently fakes a command.

That is good for learning. It also means you must read the error and check help.
Understanding Through a Language Tutor

A language tutor who accepts every mistake teaches a private language. A tutor who corrects you teaches the language other people speak.

NetSim corrects you.
Discovering Commands with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Translate the Intent

Ask the AI to turn an intent into a command.

Intent: give pc1 the address 10.0.1.10/24 on eth0 and make 10.0.1.1 the
default gateway.

Write the iproute2 commands. Explain what each command changes and how
you would verify it.

A good answer includes the verification.

Exploration 2: Read the Error

Ask what an unsupported command means.

NetSim returns: netsim: "ip route show table all" is not supported.
Explain what the student should do next. Do not suggest guessing.

The next step is help, not a workaround.

Exploration 3: Compare Inspector and Terminal

Ask whether the two paths are equivalent.

Adding an address in the Inspector and with ip addr add both use the same
engine. Explain why that matters for teaching and for the exported
configuration.

The interface is not a separate model.
From Concept to Practice

A configuration record:

Device Command Purpose Verification
pc1 ip addr add ... Address ip addr show
pc1 ip route add default ... Gateway ip route
r1 sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 Forwarding sysctl
fw1 nft add rule ... Policy nft list ruleset
Build Task
Configure one host and one router from the terminal. Verify every change with a show command. Then break one command on purpose and read the error.
Classroom Connection
The loud error is a teaching feature. Students learn the real subset and the habit of checking.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 3.1 (Level 1). Add an address and verify it. Exercise 3.2 (Level 2). Add a default route. Exercise 3.3 (Level 3). Turn on forwarding. Exercise 3.4 (Level 4). Write one nft rule and one iptables rule. Exercise 3.5 (Level 5). Explain why unsupported syntax should fail.
Chapter Summary

• NetSim uses a curated subset of real syntax.
  • Unsupported commands fail loudly.
  • The Inspector and terminal use the same engine.
  • Verify every change.
  • help is the first troubleshooting step.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Added an address
  • [ ] Added a route
  • [ ] Enabled forwarding
  • [ ] Read one error
  • [ ] Verified with a show command
Your Learning Journal

1. Which command was easiest to mistype?
  2. What did the error teach you?
  3. Why is a loud error better than a silent fake?
Next Steps
The devices are configured. The next chapter follows a packet.
A packet is a sequence of decisions, and NetSim lets you stop at every one.
The Concept First

A ping from pc1 to pc2 is not one event. It is a chain:

  1. The host checks whether the destination is local.
  2. If local, it needs the destination MAC. ARP resolves it.
  3. If remote, it sends to the default gateway and needs the gateway MAC.
  4. The switch learns the source MAC and forwards the frame.
  5. The router decrements TTL, checks the route and forwards.
  6. The destination replies, and the return path repeats.

NetSim animates ARP in amber, ICMP in blue, TCP in green and UDP in purple. A red ring flashes where a firewall drops a packet.

The first ping is often slower because ARP must resolve the MAC. The second is faster because the neighbour table is warm.
Understanding Through a Delivery Route

A parcel moves through a pickup, a depot, a flight and a local van. Each stage has a decision and a record.

A packet is the parcel. The tables are the depot records.
Discovering the Path with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Predict the Path

Ask the AI to trace a packet before you run it.

pc1 192.168.1.10/24, gateway 192.168.1.1
r1 eth0 192.168.1.1/24, eth1 192.168.2.1/24
pc2 192.168.2.20/24, gateway 192.168.2.1

Predict the path of ping from pc1 to pc2. Include ARP, the switch, the
router, TTL and the return path.

The prediction makes the animation meaningful.

Exploration 2: Find the Drop

Ask how to explain a failed ping.

A ping fails. The host has an address, the link is up, and the firewall
log shows a drop. List the evidence you would collect in order and the
rule you would check.

The firewall log names the verdict. The route table shows the path.

Exploration 3: Test the First-Ping Effect

Ask why the first ping differs.

The first ping takes longer than the second. Explain why, and what you
would clear to reproduce the first-ping behaviour.

The ARP cache is the answer.
From Concept to Practice

A packet record:

Step Device Decision Evidence
1 pc1 Remote destination ip route
2 pc1 Need gateway MAC ARP request
3 sw1 Learn and forward MAC table
4 r1 TTL and route ip route
5 pc2 Reply ip neigh
Build Task
Run a ping with the simulation paused. Step through the packets. Record the ARP request, the ICMP echo, the reply and the tables that changed.
Classroom Connection
The pause button is the lesson. Students can point at the packet and explain the decision before it moves.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 4.1 (Level 1). Trace a local ping. Exercise 4.2 (Level 2). Trace a routed ping. Exercise 4.3 (Level 3). Explain the first-ping delay. Exercise 4.4 (Level 4). Find the rule behind a firewall drop. Exercise 4.5 (Level 5). Draw the forward and return paths.
Chapter Summary

• A packet is a chain of decisions.
  • ARP resolves a MAC before a frame can be sent.
  • Switches learn and forward; routers route and decrement TTL.
  • The firewall log names the rule.
  • Pause and step to explain.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Predicted a path
  • [ ] Stepped through a ping
  • [ ] Found the ARP exchange
  • [ ] Read a table
  • [ ] Explained a drop
Your Learning Journal

1. Which decision surprised you?
  2. What did the table show that the animation did not?
  3. Where would you pause next time?
Next Steps
The packet is visible. The next chapter tests policy with firewalls.

questions.prompt: Why can NetSim explain a packet drop that a real kernel cannot?
options: It is a deterministic discrete-event simulator with an inspectable rule model
It captures packets from the host
questions.explanation: The simulation can name the event, the interface and the matching rule.

questions.prompt: Which device type has four interfaces and forwards IPv4?
questions.explanation: A firewall is a router with nftables base chains declared.

questions.prompt: What does NetSim do with unsupported syntax?
options: It errors loudly and names the command as unsupported
questions.explanation: Real syntax is the promise. A loud error is better than a fake command.

questions.prompt: Why is the first ping often slower than the second?
options: ARP must resolve the destination or gateway MAC first
questions.explanation: The neighbour table is warm after the first exchange.

questions.prompt: What does the switch use to forward a frame?
questions.explanation: The switch learns source MACs and forwards by destination MAC.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum useful topology for a two-host ping?
questions.explanation: Start with the smallest topology that tests the question.

blocks.html: A firewall is a sequence of rules, and NetSim can name the rule that decided.
The Concept First

NetSim firewalls support nft and iptables front-ends over one internal rule model. A rule added in one dialect lists in both.

The model covers:

  • input, forward and output chains
  • accept, drop and reject verdicts
  • chain policies
  • connection tracking (ct state new,established,related)
  • NAT: masquerade, SNAT and DNAT port forwarding

A firewall is a router with base chains declared. It also has a per-device log that names the exact rule behind every verdict.

DROP is silent. REJECT sends an ICMP unreachable or a TCP reset. The difference matters: a client sees a timeout for a drop and a refusal for a reject.
Understanding Through a Nightclub Door

A door policy is an ordered list. The first matching rule decides. A broad accept at the top makes every later drop irrelevant.

A firewall is the door. The log is the bouncer's note.
Discovering Firewalls with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Write the Policy First

Ask the AI to state the policy in plain language.

A LAN may reach the internet. The internet may reach the public web
server on tcp/80 only. Everything else is dropped.

Write the firewall policy in plain language, then the nftables rules.
Do not write the rules first.

The policy is the intent. The rules are the implementation.

Exploration 2: Test DROP and REJECT

Ask how the client sees each.

Compare a silent drop and a reject for tcp/22 from the internet. What does
the client see, what does the log show and which verdict is appropriate?

A drop is quiet; a reject is a message.

Exploration 3: Read the Verdict

Ask how to explain a blocked packet.

A packet was dropped. List the evidence you would collect: chain, rule,
source, destination, protocol and state. Explain why the log is better
than guessing.

The log is the explanation.
From Concept to Practice

A firewall record:

Field Entry
Device fw1
Chain forward
Policy drop
Rule allow LAN to WAN, allow tcp/80 in
State established,related
Log rule ID and verdict
Test allowed path and denied path
Build Task
Start with a default-deny policy. Allow the LAN out and tcp/80 in. Test both the allowed and denied paths. Read the log for the denial.
Classroom Connection
Firewalls are where students learn that order and policy are design decisions. The log makes the decision visible.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 5.1 (Level 1). Name the three chains. Exercise 5.2 (Level 2). Write a default-deny policy. Exercise 5.3 (Level 3). Add a stateful allow rule. Exercise 5.4 (Level 4). Compare DROP and REJECT. Exercise 5.5 (Level 5). Add DNAT to a DMZ web server and test it.
Chapter Summary

• NetSim firewalls use nft and iptables over one model.
  • Chains, policies and verdicts decide the packet.
  • Stateful rules allow replies.
  • DROP and REJECT look different to the client.
  • The log names the rule.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Wrote the policy
  • [ ] Set default deny
  • [ ] Allowed one path
  • [ ] Denied another
  • [ ] Read the log
Your Learning Journal

1. Which rule was easiest to misorder?
  2. What did the client see for a drop?
  3. When would you use REJECT?
Next Steps
The firewall decides. The next chapter adds the services that depend on it.
DHCP, DNS and HTTP are ordinary packets. That is why they can be firewalled.
The Concept First

NetSim runs services as real packet exchanges:

  • DHCP: dhclient sends DISCOVER, receives OFFER, sends REQUEST and receives ACK. The client installs the address, default route and nameserver.
  • DNS: an A-record server answers dig over UDP/53. Hostname resolution is wired into ping, traceroute, nc and curl.
  • HTTP: a configurable web server answers curl over the simulated TCP handshake.
  • TCP/UDP: nc tests ports, nc -l listens, ss and conntrack -L show state.

All service traffic animates on the wire. Block UDP/67 and DHCP dies. Block UDP/53 and DNS dies. Block TCP/80 and the web dies.
Understanding Through a Postal Service

DHCP is the address assignment desk. DNS is the directory. HTTP is the parcel.

Each has a protocol, a server and a failure mode.
Discovering Services with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Trace DHCP

Ask the AI to label the four packets.

dhclient runs on pc2 against a DHCP server. List the four packets, the
direction, the transport and what the client installs after the ACK.

A good answer names DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST and ACK.

Exploration 2: Break DNS

Ask what happens when UDP/53 is blocked.

A firewall drops udp/53 between pc2 and the DNS server. Explain what
happens to dig, ping by name and curl by name. What still works by IP?

The failure is specific, not "the network is down".

Exploration 3: Test the Web

Ask how to read a curl failure.

curl http://web.lan/ fails. List the checks in order: DNS, route, TCP
connect, firewall and server. Explain what each result would tell you.

A structured diagnosis beats guessing.
From Concept to Practice

A service record:

Service Client Server Port Evidence
DHCP pc2 dhcp UDP/67 ip addr, lease
DNS pc2 dns UDP/53 dig
HTTP pc2 web TCP/80 curl -v
Test pc2 target TCP nc
Build Task
Run dhclient, then dig, then curl. Capture the packets and the state each step installs.
Classroom Connection
Services teach dependency. A web request depends on DNS, routing and TCP. The failure points are the lesson.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 6.1 (Level 1). Name the four DHCP packets. Exercise 6.2 (Level 2). Resolve a name with dig. Exercise 6.3 (Level 3). Fetch a page with curl. Exercise 6.4 (Level 4). Block DNS and explain the failures. Exercise 6.5 (Level 5). Diagnose a curl failure in order.
Chapter Summary

• Services are packet exchanges.
  • DHCP assigns address, route and nameserver.
  • DNS resolves names over UDP/53.
  • HTTP runs over TCP.
  • Service traffic can be firewalled.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Traced DHCP
  • [ ] Ran dig
  • [ ] Ran curl
  • [ ] Blocked one service
  • [ ] Diagnosed one failure
Your Learning Journal

1. Which service was easiest to break?
  2. What did the client install?
  3. Where did the failure appear first?
Next Steps
The services work. The next chapter uses the bundled labs and auto-grader.
A lab is a starting topology, a sequence of steps and objectives the simulator can test.
The Concept First

NetSim ships five guided labs:

  1. Static addressing and ARP
  2. Routing between networks
  3. Build a stateful firewall
  4. DHCP, DNS and the web
  5. Harden a vulnerable network

Each lab has steps, objectives and quizzes. The Check objectives button runs the checks against the live simulation using real packets. Students see the grader's probes animate.

The checks are passive or active. Passive checks read device state, such as an interface address or a firewall policy. Active checks send packets, such as a ping, a TCP connect, a DNS query or an HTTP fetch.

A lab is not a quiz with a network attached. It is a scenario with evidence.
Understanding Through a Driving Test

A driving test does not ask whether you read the manual. It watches you drive.

A NetSim lab watches the packets.
Discovering the Labs with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Map Lab to Concept

Ask the AI to match each lab to a concept.

Here are the five NetSim labs:
[paste them]

For each, name the main concept and one check that proves it. Explain
why a passive check is not enough on its own.

Active checks prove behaviour; passive checks prove configuration.

Exploration 2: Prove the Problem

Ask why a security lab checks the vulnerability first.

Lab 5 asks students to confirm the exposure before they harden it.
Explain why this is better than starting with the fix. What does it
teach about evidence?

The first objective establishes the current state.

Exploration 3: Choose the Verdict

Ask about filtered versus refused.

A firewall drops tcp/22 silently. Another rejects it. Which check should
a hardening lab use, and what does the student learn from the difference?

A silent drop is usually the stronger security outcome.
From Concept to Practice

A lab record:

Lab Concept Objective Check
1 Addressing and ARP Hosts can ping ping
2 Routing Packet crosses router ping, traceroute
3 Stateful firewall LAN out, internet in blocked tcp, fw-policy
4 Services DHCP, DNS, HTTP work dns, http
5 Hardening Public web reachable, rest filtered tcp filtered
Build Task
Complete Lab 1 and export the attempt. Then import it and check the objectives again.
Classroom Connection
Auto-grading gives immediate feedback. It is formative, not a proctored exam. The attempt file is editable, so use it for learning and evidence, not high-stakes assessment.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 7.1 (Level 1). Name the five labs. Exercise 7.2 (Level 2). Complete Lab 1. Exercise 7.3 (Level 3). Explain one active check. Exercise 7.4 (Level 4). Compare filtered and refused. Exercise 7.5 (Level 5). Export, import and regrade an attempt.
Chapter Summary

• A lab is a topology, steps and objectives.
  • Active checks send packets; passive checks read state.
  • The grader's probes animate.
  • Prove the problem before the fix.
  • Auto-grading is formative.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Completed one lab
  • [ ] Read an objective
  • [ ] Watched a probe
  • [ ] Exported an attempt
  • [ ] Regraded it
Your Learning Journal

1. Which objective was clearest?
  2. What did the probe prove?
  3. Where is auto-grading weakest?
Next Steps
The labs work. The next chapter designs one.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between DROP and REJECT?
options: DROP is silent; REJECT sends a refusal or unreachable
DROP sends a reset; REJECT is silent
questions.explanation: The client sees a timeout for DROP and a refusal for REJECT.

questions.prompt: What does connection tracking enable?
options: Replies to established connections without a separate inbound rule
questions.explanation: Stateful rules allow the return path.

questions.prompt: What are the four DHCP packets?
questions.explanation: The client discovers, receives an offer, requests it and is acknowledged.

questions.prompt: What happens when UDP/53 is blocked?
options: DNS resolution fails; IP connectivity may still work
questions.explanation: Service failures are specific, not a general network outage.

questions.prompt: What is an active lab check?
options: A check that sends a real packet and watches the result
A check that reads an interface address
questions.explanation: Active checks produce behaviour evidence and animate the probe.

questions.prompt: Why does Lab 5 prove the exposure before the fix?
options: The first objective establishes the baseline the student is asked to change
questions.explanation: Evidence of the problem comes before evidence of the fix.

questions.prompt: Why is auto-grading formative rather than proctored?
options: The attempt file is editable and can be changed
questions.explanation: Use it for feedback and evidence, not high-stakes assessment.

blocks.prompt: A firewall ruleset has a broad ACCEPT near the top and the correct DROP rules below it. The test suite shows the allowed path working. The student says the firewall is finished. Choose your next move.

options.label: Check which rules are reached, move the broad accept, and test the denied path
options.outcome: The broad accept was shadowing every later drop. After moving it, the allowed path still works and the denied path is blocked. The log names the rule for each verdict.
options.feedback: A ruleset is a sequence. The first match wins, and a rule that is never reached does nothing.

options.label: Accept the result because the allowed path works
options.outcome: The firewall passes the only test the student ran. The rules that were supposed to block traffic are never reached.
options.feedback: Test the denied path. The allowed path proves the firewall is not blocking everything.

options.label: Add more drop rules below the broad accept
options.outcome: The new rules are also shadowed. The ruleset grows and the policy does not change.

options.label: Set the policy to drop and remove all rules
options.outcome: The allowed path stops working. The firewall is now secure and useless. The policy needs both the default and the exceptions.
options.feedback: Default deny is a starting point, not a complete policy.

blocks.debrief: Read the ruleset in order, find the shadowed rules, test both paths and let the log explain the verdict.

lessons.title: Design a Lab That Checks the Right Thing

blocks.html: An objective is a claim about the network, written so the simulator can test it.
The Concept First

A NetSim objective has an id, a student-facing label and a check. The check is passive or active.

Common check types:

  • iface-ip: an interface has an address or an address in a subnet.
  • default-route: a default route exists, optionally via a gateway.
  • forwarding: IP forwarding matches the expected value.
  • fw-policy: a chain policy matches.
  • ping: an ICMP echo succeeds or fails.
  • tcp: a TCP connect is open, refused or filtered.
  • dns: a name resolves or returns NXDOMAIN.
  • http: a GET succeeds, optionally with a required string.

The design question is not "what did I teach?" It is "what evidence would prove the student did it?"
Understanding Through a Building Inspection

An inspector does not ask whether the builder read the code. The inspector checks the exit, the alarm and the record.

A lab objective is the check. The step is the instruction.
Discovering Objectives with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Turn a Step into a Check

Ask the AI to choose a check.

Step: "Give pc1 the address 192.168.1.10/24 on eth0."
Write the objective and the check. Then write a second objective that
proves the host can reach its gateway.

One check for configuration, one for behaviour.

Exploration 2: Prove the Problem

Ask for a vulnerability-first objective.

A lab asks students to harden a network. Write an objective that passes
while the vulnerability exists, then the objective that passes after the
fix. Explain the order.

The first objective establishes the baseline.

Exploration 3: Find the Weak Check

Ask what a check misses.

A lab checks that tcp/22 is filtered from the internet. What does that
not prove? Write a second check that closes the gap.

A check is evidence for one claim, not all claims.
From Concept to Practice

An objective record:

Field Entry
ID l6-ip

A lab is a JSON file. That is the whole distribution mechanism.
The Concept First

A NetSim lab file has the same shape as a topology, plus a top-level lab object:

{
  "app": "netsim",
  "version": 1,
  "devices": [],
  "links": [],
  "lab": {
    "id": "my-lab",
    "title": "Lab 6 - My topic",
    "blurb": "One line for the Labs menu.",
    "steps": []
  }
}

A step has a title, a body, objectives and an optional quiz. A quiz answer is a zero-based index.

The recommended authoring path:

  1. Build the starting topology in NetSim.
  2. Export the topology JSON.
  3. Add the lab block.
  4. Import it back and test as a student.
  5. Iterate until every objective goes green at the right time.
  6. Distribute the file or a share link.
Understanding Through a Lesson Plan
A lesson plan has objectives, activities and a check. A lab file is the same, with a topology attached.
Discovering the Format with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Build the Skeleton

Ask the AI to draft the JSON.

Write a NetSim lab skeleton for a two-host addressing lab. Include the
lab id, title, blurb, one step with a title, body, two objectives and
one quiz question. Use JSON, not prose.

A skeleton is easier to review than a blank file.

Exploration 2: Test the Check

Ask what could go wrong.

A lab objective uses `iface-ip` with `inSubnet`. List the ways it could
pass without the student understanding subnetting. Write a stronger
second check.

A check is not a lesson.

Exploration 3: Plan Distribution

Ask how to hand it out.

Compare distributing a lab as a JSON file, a share link and a bundled
lab in the repository. Include the trade-offs for updating, versioning
and collecting attempts.

Each route has a maintenance cost.

Chapter Summary

• A lab is a topology plus a lab block.
  • Steps contain objectives and quizzes.
  • Build the topology visually, then add the JSON.
  • Test as a student before distributing.

The lab is distributed. The final chapter exports the design to real systems.
A simulation is useful when the design can leave it.
The Concept First

NetSim exports more than a picture:

  • Device config bundle (.zip): per-device setup.sh, nftables.conf and dnsmasq.conf.
  • Containerlab topology: a .clab.yml with Linux nodes and firewall rules.
  • Docker Compose: an approximate L2 topology.
  • SVG/PNG diagrams: documentation-grade topology images.
  • Printable HTML report: diagram, inventory, cabling, routing tables, DHCP/DNS and firewall rulesets.

The generated configs are validated in CI against the real nft and dnsmasq binaries. That is the bridge from the simulator to a real machine.

The export is not a promise that the real network will behave identically. It is a starting point that preserves the design.
Understanding Through a Building Plan

A building plan is not the building. It is the document a builder can follow.

The export is the plan. The real network is the building.
Discovering Exports with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Choose the Export

Ask which export fits the task.

A team wants to hand a firewall design to an engineer, run it in a lab,
and include it in a report. Which NetSim exports fit each task? Explain
the limits.

Different artefacts for different readers.

Exploration 2: Review the Config

Ask what to check before running it.

Here is a generated nftables.conf:
[paste it]

List the checks before applying it to a real host: interfaces, addresses,
default policy, rule order, NAT and rollback.

A generated config is a draft until reviewed.

Exploration 3: Compare Simulation and Reality

Ask what changes.

The simulated network works. The real containerlab deployment does not.
List the differences that could explain it: interface names, kernel
settings, L2 behaviour, image versions and timing.

The export removes typing, not thinking.

Chapter Summary

• NetSim exports configs, containerlab, Compose, diagrams and reports.
  • The config bundle is the bridge to a real machine.
  • Generated configs need review.
  • The export preserves the design, not the behaviour guarantee.
  • Remove typing, not thinking.

questions.prompt: What is a lab objective?
options: A testable claim about the network with a stable ID and a check
questions.explanation: The check is passive or active and the ID keys saved progress.

questions.prompt: When should an author use an active check instead of a passive one?
options: When the claim is about behaviour, such as reachability or a filtered port
When the claim is about an interface address
When the answer is in the Inspector
When the lab has no topology
questions.explanation: Active checks send packets and watch the result.

questions.prompt: Why keep objective IDs stable?
options: Saved progress and exported attempts are keyed by the ID
questions.explanation: Renaming an ID resets the objective for every student.

options: Build the topology in the app, export the JSON, add the lab block and import it back
Write every device by hand from scratch

questions.explanation: The teacher can import it, land in the network and regrade.

questions.explanation: It is the bridge from the design to a real lab, not a promise of identical behaviour.
